attempts.raw_response: Once the seedlings emerge, move them to a spot with plenty of bright light, such as a sunny south-facing window or under grow lights. If you started multiple seeds in one container, thin them out once they develop their first set of true leaves, keeping only the strongest ones. When the seedlings reach about three inches tall and have several sets of leaves, they are ready to be transplanted into individual pots. Use a well-draining soil mix to prevent root rot. Gradually acclimate the young plants to outdoor conditions by setting them outside for a few hours each day, increasing the time over the course of a week. After the danger of frost has passed, transplant them into your garden, spacing them about two feet apart.

pair.human_continuation:
Monitor your seeds while you wait for them to sprout. Make sure the soil stays wet while you wait for them to sprout, and keep the seeds in a sunny area. After the seeds sprout, you should move the container to a location that receives plenty of direct sunlight. If no such location is available, place a fluorescent grow light about the sprouts and allow them to sit in the artificial light for eight hours a day.
Mature lavender is fairly drought-resistant, but while lavender is within its first year of growth, it needs regular watering. Normal weather conditions often suffice, but if you live in an area that is particularly dry or if you have not received much rain, you should regularly soak the soil.
pair.prefix: A heat tray often works best, but another work location may also work as long as the temperature remains around 70 degrees Fahrenheit (21 degrees Celsius). Keep the growing medium moist, but not damp, and water the seeds in the morning so that the soil can dry some before evening hits. Soil that is too damp and cool will invite fungus to grow, and fungus will destroy your seeds. Lavender seeds can take two weeks to one month to sprout.
